subject: surgery
title: Biliary surgery: acute cholecystitis, critical view of safety and bile duct injuries

steps.tx: Symptomatic cholelithiasis and **acute cholecystitis** arise from cystic duct obstruction by an impacted gallstone. Entrapped bile triggers sterile chemical inflammation, mucosal ischemia and secondary bacterial infection by enteric coliforms. Ultrasonography is the diagnostic modality of choice, demonstrating gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening greater than four millimeters, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy sign. Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within seventy-two hours is the definitive management.
steps.say: Acute cholecystitis arises from cystic duct obstruction by an impacted gallstone. Entrapped bile triggers inflammation, mucosal ischemia and bacterial infection. Ultrasonography is the diagnostic test of choice, demonstrating gallstones, wall thickening over four millimeters, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy sign. Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is definitive.

rows: Gallstones present, normal wall thickness, no fluid
Thickened wall > 4 mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy
Dilated CBD > 6 mm, elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin
Charcot triad: fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain

steps.tx: During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, achieving Strasberg **critical view of safety** is the mandatory standard of care to prevent catastrophic common bile duct injury. It requires three anatomical criteria: the hepatocystic triangle must be completely cleared of all fat and fibrous tissue; the lower third of the gallbladder must be dissected off the cystic plate; and only two structures—the cystic duct and cystic artery—must be seen entering the gallbladder.
steps.say: Achieving the Strasberg critical view of safety is the mandatory standard to prevent bile duct injury during laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Three criteria must be met: clearing the hepatocystic triangle of all fat and fibrous tissue, mobilizing the lower third of gallbladder off the liver bed, and seeing only two structures enter the gallbladder.

steps.tx: Iatrogenic **bile duct injury** is classified according to the Strasberg-Bismuth grading system. Strasberg type A involves bile leakage from small cystic duct or minor liver bed ducts. Type D represents partial lateral laceration of a major bile duct. Type E injuries involve complete transection or occlusion of the common hepatic or main bile duct. When extensive thermal injury or tissue loss occurs, definitive reconstruction requires a tension-free Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy.
steps.say: Iatrogenic bile duct injury is classified by the Strasberg-Bismuth system. Type A involves leakage from the cystic duct or liver bed. Type D represents lateral laceration of a major duct. Type E involves complete transection of the main bile duct. Extensive injuries require definitive reconstruction with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy.

left.title: Strasberg Type A-D injuries
points: Minor duct leaks or partial lacerations
Often managed with ERCP and biliary stenting

right.title: Strasberg Type E injuries
points: Complete transection of common hepatic/bile duct
Misidentification of common duct as cystic duct
Risk of recurrent cholangitis and anastomotic stricture

steps.tx: Acute ascending **cholangitis** is a life-threatening infection resulting from biliary stasis and high intraductal pressure. Charcot triad comprises fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Progression to Reynolds pentad adds septic shock and altered mental status. Initial management demands aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and emergency biliary decompression via endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with biliary sphincterotomy and stenting.
